Summarize how each item behaved

item_report.Rd

Produces a diagnostic data frame where each row is one item, or each row is one item and label, summarizing how each item behaved across the corpus. Each column answers a different question about whether an item is usable.

It is purely descriptive, meaning no column here reports whether an item is correct. A confident, low-leakage item can still be measuring something other than the construct. inspect_cases() is what answers that, by showing the documents.

Usage

item_report(results, target = NULL, order = c("declared", "size"))

Arguments

results

A fathom_results object from measure() or read_checkpoints().

target

A string naming the label counted as endorsement. Defaults to the first (e.g., "yes" in an instrument where "yes" was written first before "no"). Used by the endorsement shape only.

order

A string setting how labels are ordered within a question. "declared", the default, is the order the instrument wrote them, which for an ordered scale is the scale and which every other part of the package already uses. "size" puts the most frequent winner first, which is the reading for unordered categories. No effect on the endorsement shape, which has no label rows.

Value

A tibble in one of three shapes, chosen as described below. Items come back in the order the instrument declares them rather than alphabetically, and an item present in the results but absent from the instrument sorts after the declared ones.

Endorsement shape

Exactly two labels and no scores. One row per item.

  • item is the question name.

  • n counts the documents scored on this item. Failed calls are excluded, so this can sit below the corpus size.

  • endorse_renorm is the share of those documents where target reached 0.5 on prob_renorm, the probability after the labels have been rescaled to sum to 1. Reaching it means the label beat the other one.

  • n_endorse_renorm is the count behind endorse_renorm. Its denominator is n minus the documents where no label appeared, which have no renormalized probability. That count is pct_both_absent times n, and is 0 whenever pct_both_absent is.

  • endorse is the same cut on prob, the probability against everything the model could have written. Reaching it means the model committed to the label.

  • n_endorse is the count behind endorse. Its denominator is n.

  • mean_prob is the mean prob on target, so it belongs to endorse rather than to endorse_renorm. It separates from endorse only when the probabilities cluster near the 0.5 cut. When they all sit near 0 or 1 the two agree almost exactly, so the gap between them says how far the endorsements were from being coin flips.

  • pct_extreme_renorm is the share of renormalized probabilities at or beyond 0.01 and 0.99, so it asks how the on-label mass was shaped rather than how much of it there was. This is the substantive one, for the same reason endorse_renorm is. It is not unconditionally the safer one. A document that answered almost entirely outside the label set can leave this denominator, read as graded, or read as certain, depending on how its residue fell.

  • pct_extreme is the share of raw probabilities at or beyond 0.01 and 0.99. Reads prob, so it cannot separate a decisive answer from one that never entered the label set, since both put every label at the floor or the ceiling. Read it against pct_extreme_renorm and max_prob_other rather than alone. Near 1 means almost every answer came back at one end or the other, so these are labels in numeric clothing. Reporting them as degrees of confidence would claim more than they carry.

  • pct_both_absent is the share of documents where no label appeared at position 1. That is a template or prompt failure rather than a low score. A broken chat template registers in n_off_label rather than here, because the labels stay in the distribution at trace mass underneath whatever the template wrote first, which leaves pct_both_absent at 0 while every answer is unusable.

  • max_prob_other is the most probability the model ever placed on tokens that were none of your labels, anywhere in the corpus. Leaked mass, in the term used elsewhere in these docs.

  • min_top1 is the least confident single answer in the corpus. For each document, take the probability of whichever token the model was most likely to write, label or not. This is the smallest of those. High values do not mean the item is correct.

  • n_off_label counts the documents where the emitted token matched no label. It is judged by the same rule scoring uses, so a token that opens a label counts as that label and a split label is not reported as off-label.

  • n_failed counts the documents whose call failed. Divided by the label count, so it counts documents rather than rows.

  • other_vs_median is max_prob_other divided by the middle value of that column across the instrument, so 2 means this item placed twice as much probability outside the labels as the typical item did. Present only for an instrument of three or more items, since a middle value across one or two carries nothing. This is the one column the item count decides. Absolute leaked mass varies by model, by language, and by how close to 0 and 1 the instrument's probabilities sit, so values are not comparable across instruments.

  • mean_expected is the average expected score across documents, which on two labels is the mean of prob_renorm on target rescaled onto the scores. Present only when the instrument carries scores. Note that mean_prob is the raw probability, so the two differ by whatever mass fell outside the labels.

Choice shape

More than two labels and no scores. One row per item and label.

  • item and label are the question and category.

  • n_won counts the documents where this label took the largest probability. A document whose distribution held none of the labels wins nothing.

  • share_won is n_won over the documents scored on that item, so the shares of an item fall short of 1 by the share that answered outside the labels.

Scored shape

Whenever the instrument carries scores and there are more than two labels. One row per item and label, the same winner distribution plus the scale.

  • item and label are the question and category.

  • score is the numeric value the instrument assigns that label.

  • n_won and share_won are as in the choice shape.

  • mean_expected is the average expected score across documents, per question. For a single document the expected score multiplies each label's value by its probability and adds them up, after those probabilities have been rescaled to sum to 1 across the labels. Because it uses every label rather than only the winner, a document the model split between two neighboring levels lands between them.

  • sd_expected is the standard deviation of the same, across documents.

Two endorsement rates

endorse and endorse_renorm count the same documents at the same cut of 0.5, and differ only in which probability they cut. Do not read the gap between them as measurement error or as disagreement between two estimates of one quantity. It is two quantities.

Neither cut is configurable. 0.5 on prob_renorm is the argmax on a two-label instrument, and threshold_sensitivity() exists to show how little the cut point matters on prob. Both are reported so the choice does not have to be made in advance.

Output shapes

Three shapes come back, and which one is decided by the labels rather than by the items. The number of items changes how many rows come back, not which columns. The test runs in this order.

  1. Exactly two labels. Endorsement shape.

  2. Otherwise, the instrument carries scores. Scored shape.

  3. Otherwise, more than two labels. Choice shape.

The label count is tested first because on two labels the scored shape reports one number, the average expected score, and drops a dozen diagnostics to do it. There is no reason to choose between them. A scored instrument of two labels reports as endorsement and gains mean_expected as a column, so the number arrives without the diagnostics leaving.

exclusive = TRUE is not itself the test. An exclusive instrument lands in the choice or scored shape because it usually has more than two labels or a scale, and an exclusive instrument of two labels reports as endorsement like any other. Equally, K separate questions sharing one scale reach the scored shape without being exclusive at all.

Nothing here decides whether your labels are ordered, and nothing can. What scores says is that an average of those numbers is defined, which is why the shape is named for the argument rather than for a measurement level. validate_sample() is where ordering is declared, by its level.

The shapes differ in row granularity as well as in columns. Endorsement gives one row per item. Choice and scored give one row per item and label, because a shared distribution has no single number per question to report. Choice and scored report a winner distribution, and leaked mass reaches them as a message rather than as a column.

target applies to the endorsement shape only, and is ignored by the other two. There is no per-label endorsement rate for a forced choice, since the labels all compete for one pool of probability, and a rate for whichever label sorted first is not a meaningful quantity.

See also

inspect_cases() for the documents behind an item, and threshold_sensitivity() for how the rates move with the cut point.

Examples

# Results from a real run ship with the package, so this needs no server.
p <- system.file("extdata", "vignette_results.rds", package = "fathom")
baked <- readRDS(p)
item_report(baked$res_indep)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 15
#>   item         n endorse_renorm n_endorse_renorm endorse n_endorse mean_prob
#>   <chr>    <int>          <dbl>            <int>   <dbl>     <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 negative   100           0.47               47    0.47        47     0.464
#> 2 positive   100           0.42               42    0.42        42     0.420
#> 3 mixed      100           0.31               31    0.31        31     0.310
#> # ℹ 8 more variables: pct_extreme_renorm <dbl>, pct_extreme <dbl>,
#> #   pct_both_absent <dbl>, max_prob_other <dbl>, min_top1 <dbl>,
#> #   n_off_label <int>, n_failed <dbl>, other_vs_median <dbl>
